template: Print debugging is the most common approach. Essentially, you insert {context} into your code to track variable states and flow. It's great for quick checks, though it can clutter your source code.
fallback: Print debugging involves adding output statements to your code to see what's happening during execution.

template: Interactive debugging is a powerhouse move. By using {context}, you can freeze the program execution at a specific line and inspect the entire memory heap in real-time.
fallback: An interactive debugger lets you pause your program and examine its state step-by-step.

template: Rubber ducking is a psychological trick! By explaining {context} to an inanimate object, you force your brain to process the logic differently, often revealing the bug yourself.
fallback: Rubber ducking is the act of explaining your code line-by-line to someone (or something) to find logic errors.

template: Remote debugging is essential when the bug only happens on a server. It allows you to connect your local IDE to {context} to diagnose issues in a production-like environment.
fallback: Remote debugging lets you debug code that is running on a different machine than your IDE.

template: Binary search debugging is a systematic way to isolate a bug. You divide the {context} in half repeatedly until you pinpoint the exact change that introduced the error.
fallback: Binary search debugging involves splitting the problematic area of code in half to narrow down the bug's location.

template: Static debugging doesn't even require running the code. It uses {context} to find potential errors, like null pointers or syntax issues, before the program ever executes.
fallback: Static analysis checks your code for errors without actually running the program.

template: Dynamic analysis happens while the program is live. It focuses on {context}, helping you catch memory leaks or performance bottlenecks that static analysis would miss.
fallback: Dynamic analysis is the process of debugging a program while it is actively running.

template: Looking at a stack trace is like reading a map of the crash. It shows you {context}, which tells you exactly which sequence of function calls led to the failure.
fallback: A stack trace provides a report of the active stack frames at a specific point in time, usually during a crash.

template: Regression debugging is all about making sure new fixes don't break old features. By checking {context}, you ensure that the system's stability is maintained after a patch.
fallback: Regression debugging ensures that recent changes haven't reintroduced old bugs or broken existing functionality.

template: Diff debugging is a great way to spot errors by comparing {context}. When you have a working version and a broken one, the differences usually point straight to the bug.
fallback: Diff debugging involves comparing two versions of a codebase to identify the specific change that caused a bug.
